# Overview {.unnumbered}

These are two self-contained computational lectures on magnetic reconnection.
Rather than deriving reconnection rates on paper alone, we test the classic
theory directly against nonlinear multi-fluid simulations of the
[GEM reconnection challenge](https://doi.org/10.1029/1999JA900449)
(Birn et al. 2001), run with [Gkeyll](https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll) and
analyzed with [postgkyl](https://github.com/gkeyllorg/postgkyl).

[Lecture 1](lectures/lecture-1-sweet-parker.ipynb): Sweet–Parker scaling in multi-fluid simulations
: Reproduce the conservation arguments of Sweet–Parker theory, mass and energy
  conservation through the current sheet, from a resistive five-moment
  simulation.

[Lecture 2](lectures/lecture-2-fast-reconnection.ipynb): What makes reconnection fast?
: Measure the reconnection rate, compare it with the Sweet–Parker prediction,
  and use an Ohm's law analysis of five- and ten-moment simulations to find what
  makes reconnection fast.

## How to use these lectures

You can read the lectures here, with all figures included. To work through
them yourself:

1. [Install Gkeyll and postgkyl](install.qmd) on your laptop.
2. [Run the two simulations](running.qmd) the lectures analyze.
3. Open the lecture notebooks in [marimo](https://marimo.io) and work through
   them with your own data.

The lecture notebooks are plain Python files in the
[`notebooks/`](https://github.com/JunoRavin/reconnection-lectures/tree/main/notebooks)
folder, and the simulation input files are in
[`inputs/`](https://github.com/JunoRavin/reconnection-lectures/tree/main/inputs).

## Prerequisites

The lectures assume familiarity with the Sweet–Parker model of reconnection and
with the basics of Python and NumPy. No prior experience with Gkeyll is needed.
